code.title: Manacher: longest palindromic substring in linear time
code.python:
s = "babcbabcbaccba"
# Pad with '#' so odd and even palindromes both get a centre cell.
t = "#" + "#".join(s) + "#"
n = len(t)
p = [0] * n                      # p[i] = palindrome radius around cell i
c = r = best = best_c = 0
for i in range(n):
    # Inside the box that ends at r: reuse the mirror cell, capped at the box edge.
    if i < r:
        p[i] = min(p[2 * c - i], r - i)
    # Expand with real comparisons; every success pushes r to the right.
    while i - p[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + p[i] + 1 < n and t[i - p[i] - 1] == t[i + p[i] + 1]:
        p[i] += 1
    if i + p[i] > r:
        c, r = i, i + p[i]
    if p[i] > best:
        best, best_c = p[i], i
start = (best_c - best) // 2     # map the padded cell back to the text
print("Text: " + s)
print("Longest palindrome: " + s[start:start + best] + " (length " + str(best) + ")")
# Time O(N): r only moves right. Space O(N) for the radius array.

followUps:
They are the same trick applied to two different questions: both keep a "box" that reaches furthest right and reuse answers already computed inside it. The Z-algorithm keeps a box [l, r] that matches a prefix and copies z[i - l]; Manacher keeps a palindrome box with centre c and copies the mirror value p[2c - i]. In both, the copied value is capped at the box edge (r - i), and real comparisons happen only beyond r, so r moves right at most N times and the total is O(N).

Example: in "abacaba", at i = 5 the box is the whole string with c = 3; the mirror is index 1, whose radius 1 is copied without comparing anything.

Use a palindromic tree (eertree): it has one node per distinct palindrome, so the answer is simply the number of nodes. This works because adding one letter creates at most one new palindrome (the longest palindromic suffix), so a string of length N has at most N distinct palindromes.

  1. Start with two roots: length −1 and length 0.
  2. For each letter s[i], walk suffix links from the last node until s[i - len - 1] == s[i].
  3. If that node has no edge for s[i], create a node of length len + 2 and count it.

Example: "abaab" creates a, b, aba, aa, baab, so the answer is 5. Time O(N) for a fixed alphabet, space O(N).

Use expand-around-centre whenever the string is short, say up to a few thousand letters, or when a simple, obviously correct solution matters more than speed. It tries each of the 2N − 1 centres and grows outwards, which is O(N²) time in the worst case (a string like "aaaa…") and O(1) extra space.

For N = 1,000 that is at most about 1,000,000 comparisons, which runs instantly, and the code is about eight lines with no padding and no mirror logic to get wrong. Switch to Manacher when N reaches 105 or more (1010 steps is too slow), or when you need the radius at every centre, for example to count all palindromic substrings.
